## Answer

**No.** We cannot conclude $A=0$ from $[A]=0$ in $K(\mathscr{C})$ for a general artinian abelian category. The key obstruction is that "artinian" does not imply "noetherian," so objects may have infinite length, and the Grothendieck group need not be free on the simple objects.

### Counterexample

Let $\mathscr{C}$ be the category of **artinian abelian groups** (equivalently, artinian $\mathbb{Z}$-modules).

**$\mathscr{C}$ is an artinian abelian category.** It is a Serre subcategory of $\mathbf{Ab}$: subquotients of artinian groups are artinian, so kernels and cokernels of morphisms in $\mathscr{C}$ remain in $\mathscr{C}$. Hence $\mathscr{C}$ is abelian, and every object is artinian by definition.

**The Prüfer $p$-group lies in $\mathscr{C}$.** Let $A = \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) = \mathbb{Z}[1/p]/\mathbb{Z}$. Its subgroups are exactly
$$0 \subset \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z} \subset \cdots \subset \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty),$$
a well-ordered ascending chain, so $A$ satisfies the descending chain condition on subgroups. Thus $A \in \mathscr{C}$.

**A self-extension kills the simple.** Multiplication by $p^n$ on $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$ is surjective (every element $a/p^m$ equals $p^n \cdot a/p^{m+n}$) with kernel $\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ (the elements of order dividing $p^n$). This gives a short exact sequence in $\mathscr{C}$:
$$0 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) \xrightarrow{\;\cdot p^n\;} \mathbb{Z}(p^\infty) \longrightarrow 0.$$

Applying the defining relation of the Grothendieck group:
$$[\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)] = [\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}] + [\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)] \quad\Longrightarrow\quad [\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}] = 0 \quad\text{in } K(\mathscr{C}).$$

Taking $n=1$:
$$[\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}] = 0 \quad\text{in } K(\mathscr{C}), \qquad \text{yet } \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} \neq 0.$$

### Why this happens

When $\mathscr{C}$ is **finite-length** (artinian *and* noetherian), Jordan–Hölder gives a well-defined map $[A] \mapsto \sum_i n_i [S_i]$ (multiplicities of simples), exhibiting $K(\mathscr{C})$ as the free abelian group on simple objects. Then $[A]=0$ forces all multiplicities to vanish, so $A=0$.

In a merely artinian category, objects like $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$ have infinite length and admit self-extensions $0 \to S \to A \to A \to 0$. The relation $[A]=[S]+[A]$ forces $[S]=0$ even though $S\neq 0$, collapsing simples in $K(\mathscr{C})$. The Grothendieck group is no longer free on simples, and the class map $A \mapsto [A]$ has nontrivial kernel.

### Conclusion

$[A]=0$ in $K(\mathscr{C})$ does **not** imply $A=0$ for an artinian abelian category. The implication holds only under the additional noetherian (finite-length) hypothesis.

### PROOF COMPLETE
